en: *The Brief Repentance of the Great Buddha*, one fascicle.
Now, those who wish to perform prostrations and repentance must first revere the Triple Gem. Why is this so?
Because the Triple Gem is the excellent field of merit for all sentient beings. If one can take refuge in them, then [sins] will be extinguished.
Measuring one's offenses,
one increases immeasurable merit;
this is how one can bring practitioners together.
Because one is free from birth and death, one attains the bliss of liberation.
Therefore, disciples such as [Name] take refuge in all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space;
we take refuge in all the Honored Dharmas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space.
Disciples take refuge in all the holy Sangha throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space.
The reason we offer this repentance today is that,
since beginningless time, while dwelling in the stage of ordinary beings, regardless of whether one is noble or lowly, our transgressions have been immeasurable.
Or one may generate offenses through the three types of action;
or give rise to transgressions through the six aspects;
or [commit them] by means of one's own improper reflection.
Or, by relying on external objects, one gives rise to defiled attachment.
In this way, the ten unwholesome paths of action increase and solidify eighty thousand gates of sensory dust.
Although the manifestations of these offenses are immeasurably vast, when summarized in brief, they do not exceed three types.
What are the three? First, afflictions; second, karma.
Third is the retribution.
These three types of dharmas can obstruct the Noble Path as well as the excellent and wondrous matters of humans and devas;
therefore, they are designated as the "three obstructions" in the sutras.
Therefore, when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach that one should rely on skillful means to repent and eliminate these three obstructions, once these three are extinguished,
the six sense faculties, the ten unwholesome actions, and even the eighty-four thousand gates of sensory dust will all become completely pure.
Therefore, today this disciple brings forth this superior, resolute mind to repent of the three desires that must be extinguished.
Regarding these three offenses, what kind of mind should be employed to cause them to be extinguished?
First, one should give rise to seven kinds of mental states as a preliminary means;
then these transgressions may be extinguished.
What are the seven?
First is shame and remorse; second is fear;
third is weary detachment.
Fourth, generating the bodhicitta;
fifth, regarding enemies and kin with equality;
sixth, being mindful of repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Seventh is the contemplation on the certainty of the nature of offenses.
First, regarding shame and remorse:
one reflects with self-reproach, "I and Śākyamuni Tathāgata were equally ordinary beings."
Now that the World-Honored One has attained enlightenment for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
we have remained together, immersed in and defiled by the six sense-objects, wandering through birth and death with no end in sight.
In this regard, this treasure is something for which one should feel ashamed and abashed;
it is something to be attached to as a source of disgrace. This is the second terror.
Since the physical, verbal, and mental actions of an ordinary person are constantly associated with transgressions,
by these causes and conditions, after the end of life, they ought to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts to undergo immeasurable suffering.
Thus, this is truly something to be astonished by, terrified of, frightened by, and alarmed at.
Third, regarding wearying detachment:
one should contemplate that within birth and death there is only impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity.
Suppose water bubbles arise and perish with great speed, revolving like the wheel of a chariot;
so too are we tormented by the eight sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, without a moment’s respite.
All of you, together, should simply observe your own bodies from head to foot.
Within it there are only thirty-six things:

hair, body hair, nails, teeth, the pus-filled sac, nasal mucus, saliva, the two internal organs (the raw and the cooked), the large intestine, the small intestine, the spleen, the kidneys, the heart, the lungs, the liver, the gallbladder, the *pāṣyā*, the fat, the grease, the membranes, the brain, the sinews, the marrow, and the feces and urine from the nine orifices that flow constantly.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"This body is a collection of manifold sufferings; all of it is impure."
What wise person would ever take delight in this body?
Since birth and death exist, these various evil dharmas are truly objects of weariness and revulsion.
Fourth, the arousal of the bodhicitta.
The Sūtra states:
"That which is called the Buddha-body of permanence and bliss is the Dharma-body;
it is born from immeasurable merit and wisdom."
It arises from the six pāramitās;
it arises from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
it arises from the seven worldly factors conducive to enlightenment.
From such various merits as these, wisdom is born.
One who wishes to obtain the body of a Tathāgata— the Buddha-body— should resolve upon bodhicitta and seek the fruit of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience),
characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which is the knowledge of all modes.
Purifying buddha-fields and bringing sentient beings to maturity,
they do not begrudge their own body, life, or wealth.
Fifth, regarding impartiality toward enemies and kin:
One gives rise to compassion for all sentient beings,
free from the notions of "self" and "other. Why is this?
If you perceive enemies and kin as distinct, this is discrimination.
Because of discrimination, various attachments to signs arise.
With the conditions of attachment to signs, all afflictions are produced.
Due to causes and conditions, one creates various evil karmas;
by reason of these evil karmas, one obtains bitter fruits.
Sixth, regarding the mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s kindness:
In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
the Tathāgata relinquished his head, eyes, marrow, brain, limbs, joints, hands, feet, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures; for our sake,
he practiced all manner of ascetic austerities.
This kindness and this virtue are truly difficult to repay.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Even if one were to carry [the Buddha] upon the crown of one's head or on both shoulders for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, one still could not repay it."
If we wish to repay the grace of the Tathāgata, we should, in this world,
through fierce diligence like that of an elephant, attain the endurance of toil and suffering;
disregarding our own bodies and lives, we shall establish the Triple Gem.
The Buddha, having mastered the Mahāyāna, extensively transforms sentient beings so that they may together enter the right path.
Seventh, regarding the contemplation of the emptiness of the nature of offenses:
they possess no real characteristic.
Arising from causes and conditions,
it exists through inversion;
since it arises from causes and conditions, it can likewise be extinguished by means of causes and conditions.
That which arises from causes and conditions is produced without cause by associating with evil friends;
that which ceases from causes and conditions is likewise.
This refers to the present practice of repenting with a settled mind.
Therefore, the sutra says:
"The characteristics of this transgression do not reside within."
They do not exist in between.
Therefore, all these offenses arise from what is fundamentally empty.
The seven types of mind, such as that of the Tathāgata, are already like the characteristics of conditions.
The Buddhas and sages of the ten directions raise their joined palms in reverence;
they present their most sincere and profound remorse, reforming themselves to the core of their hearts and livers, and cleansing their very entrails.
When one repents in such a manner, what transgression is there that will not be extinguished?
What obstacle could possibly remain uneliminated? If,
moreover, you continue thus in a state of aimless wandering and sluggishness, with an empty mind and merely exhausting your own body—
what hindrance is there in this?
Furthermore, human life is impermanent, like a flickering candle; if one breath does not return, one will immediately head toward the ashes and the bitter retributions of the three miserable realms.
One must receive these consequences in this very body; therefore, one should quickly calculate and strive for liberation by means of wealth, treasures, and goods.
In the profound and obscure darkness, there is no set time for grace or pardon.
I alone am beset by this suffering with no one to rely upon;
do not say that such a crime does not exist within my present life.
For this reason, one is unable to cultivate the practice of repentance.
As it is said in the sutras:
"In the lifting and moving of every step, there is nothing that is not sin for the ordinary person."
Furthermore, throughout successive births, immeasurable evil karmas will all be fully accomplished,
pursuing the practitioner like a shadow following a form;
if one lacks shame and remorse, these evils will deepen day by day.
Therefore, they harbor the defects of ignorance;
the Buddha’s teachings do not permit the confession of past sins, yet this is what Vimalakīrti esteemed.
Consequently, their wisdom has long been submerged in the ocean of suffering.
This is due to concealment.
Therefore, the disciples today openly confess and repent according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, because we have mutually relied upon one another and because of afflictions, we have given rise to evil karma.
Because of the causes and conditions of evil karma, one obtains the suffering of its fruit.
Therefore, today, with the utmost sincerity, disciples should first repent of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, these afflictions are censured in various ways by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble beings who have entered into the principle;
they also invite these afflictions to become their enemies. Why is this?
Because they sever the life-root of sentient beings' wisdom;
because they also summon this torrential river of afflictions that can sweep sentient beings away into the great ocean of suffering of birth and death;
and because they also summon these afflictions to serve as fetters and shackles that bind sentient beings within the prison of birth and death, preventing them from escaping.

One should know that it is because of the afflictions that beings are bound together within the six realms of existence, such that birth and death continue without end, evil karma is inexhaustible, and suffering never ceases.
All of this is the fault and calamity of the afflictions.
Therefore, today this disciple, with this superior mind of goodness, takes refuge in the Buddha.
Likewise, in all the Three Jewels throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space in the ten directions;
from the beginningless past until this day, this disciple [has taken refuge].
Whether receiving retribution among humans or devas,
this mind-consciousness constantly harbors folly,
sometimes filling the breast and bosom to overflowing.
Or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the characteristics of the three poisons;
or one may create the causes for all manner of offenses due to the three outflows;
or one may encounter the commission of all manner of offenses.
Or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to sensation;
or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the three types of suffering;
or one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the three provisional aggregates.
Or, due to craving for the three realms of existence, one commits all manner of transgressions.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless, causing affliction and turmoil for all beings within the six destinies and four modes of birth.
Now, with shame and remorse, I confess them all.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, the disciple has,
due to the four stations of consciousness, committed all manner of transgressions;
or, due to the four floods, committed all manner of transgressions.
Or, one may commit all transgressions due to the four graspings acting as causes; or due to the four attachments acting as causes;
or due to the four conditions acting as causes;
or due to the four great elements acting as causes.
Whether through the four bonds one has committed all manner of transgressions,
or through the four nutriments one has committed all manner of transgressions,
or through the four modes of birth— one shall repent of them all.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day, the disciple may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the afflictions of the five stages of abiding (pañca-vāsanā-bhūmi),
or may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the five modes of sensation (pañca-vedanā).
Or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the five hindrances;
or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the five types of stinginess;
or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the five views.
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the five types of mind;
such are the afflictions of these transgressions.
